Sliding-Window Transition Entropy Trajectory

Source: R/transition_entropy.R
entropy_trajectory.Rd

entropy_trajectory() tracks transition entropy over time: it forms the transitions within each actor's sequence of an event log, pools them in time order, and slides a window of a fixed number of transitions across the stream, giving one entropy estimate per window. A group column gives one trajectory per group. This turns transition entropy from a snapshot into a process measure, as Krejtz et al. (2025) do when they track gaze transition entropy through the phases of a task.

A falling trajectory means the transitions become more predictable (routinisation), a rising one less predictable (exploration), and a level shift marks a change of phase. Each window's estimate rests on window transitions, and with the default step neighbouring windows share four fifths of them, so their estimates are not independent: read the smoothed trend of plot() rather than single windows. For the whole-process value with credible intervals, use transition_entropy() and entropy_bayes().

Usage

entropy_trajectory(
  data,
  action,
  actor = NULL,
  time = NULL,
  group = NULL,
  window = 500L,
  step = NULL,
  base = 2
)

# S3 method for class 'net_entropy_trajectory'
print(x, digits = 3, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_entropy_trajectory'
summary(object, ...)

# S3 method for class 'net_entropy_trajectory'
plot(
  x,
  normalized = FALSE,
  span = 0.4,
  title = "Transition entropy over time",
  ...
)

Arguments

data

An event log: a data frame with one row per event.

action

The column holding each event's state.

actor

The column identifying sequences: transitions are formed only between consecutive events of the same actor (within the same group). Default NULL, which reads the data as one sequence.

time

The timestamp column, which orders the events within each actor and places the windows on a time axis. Default NULL, which keeps the row order and uses the row number of the event that ends each transition as the axis. The column must be numeric, a Date or a POSIXct; a character timestamp fails, so parse it first.

group

A column splitting the data into parallel trajectories (for example a condition or an achievement level), each with its own windows. Default NULL (one trajectory, labelled "all").

window

The number of transitions per window, at least 10. Default 500.

step

The number of transitions between the starts of consecutive windows. Default NULL, which uses window %/% 5 (at least 1).

base

The logarithm base, which sets the unit: 2 (default) for bits. Any positive number other than 1.

x

For the print() and plot() methods: an entropy_trajectory() result.

digits

For print(): decimal places of the entropies. Default 3.

...

For the print(), summary() and plot() methods: not used.

object

For summary(): an entropy_trajectory() result.

normalized

For plot(): whether to draw entropy_norm instead of the raw entropy. Default FALSE.

span

For plot(): the loess span of the trend line. Default 0.4.

title

For plot(): the plot title. Default "Transition entropy over time".

Value

A net_entropy_trajectory object. print() shows each group's number of windows and its mean and range of entropy, and returns its input invisibly. summary() returns a data frame with one row per group: group, windows, the mean, sd, min and max of the window entropies, the entropy of the first and last windows, and their difference change (negative when the transitions became more predictable). plot() returns a ggplot with the per-window entropy as faint lines and a loess-smoothed trend (with its standard-error band) per group, in Okabe-Ito colours. The object's fields:

trajectory

Data frame, one row per window: group, window (index within the group), time (the window's midpoint; a row number when there is no time column), time_start and time_end (the time, or row number, of the window's first and last transition), n_transitions, n_states (distinct states in the window), entropy (in base units per transition) and entropy_norm (divided by \(\log_b\) of the window's number of states, floored at 2 states so the ceiling is never zero; in \([0, 1]\)).

window, step, base

The settings used.

states

The states of the whole log.

Details

Each window's entropy is the empirical conditional entropy \(-\sum_{ij} (n_{ij}/N) \log_b(n_{ij}/n_{i\cdot})\), which weights rows by their observed occupancy rather than by the stationary distribution from the eigenvector. Within a short window the chain is often not ergodic (absorbing fragments, unvisited states), where that eigenvector is undefined or misleading; the empirical estimator is the standard windowed choice and converges to the stationary entropy rate over long stationary stretches.

The transitions of all actors are pooled in time order within each group (ties broken by actor, then by input order). A window shorter than window at the end of a stream is dropped; a group whose stream is shorter than window gets one window covering all of it, with a warning. Fewer than two transitions in all raise an error.

References

Krejtz, K., Hughes, C.J., Stasiak, I., Duchowski, A., & Krejtz, I. (2025). Real-Time Mobile Transition Matrix Entropy Based on Eye and Head Movements. ETRA '25. doi:10.1145/3715669.3723128

Cover, T.M. & Thomas, J.A. (2006). Elements of Information Theory, 2nd ed. Wiley.

See also

transition_entropy for the whole-process snapshot, entropy_bayes for credible intervals on it.

Examples

tr <- entropy_trajectory(group_regulation_long,
                         action = "Action", actor = "Actor",
                         time = "Time", group = "Achiever")
tr
#> Entropy Trajectory (9 states; window 500 transitions, step 100)
#> 
#>   High:        123 windows   mean 2.286   range [2.175, 2.394]
#>   Low:         124 windows   mean 2.294   range [2.143, 2.437]
#> 
#> Use plot() for the trajectory, summary() for per-group statistics.
summary(tr)
#>   group windows     mean         sd      min      max    first     last
#> 1  High     123 2.285872 0.04313978 2.175275 2.394429 2.309764 2.301800
#> 2   Low     124 2.294082 0.05803398 2.142537 2.436502 2.233659 2.347734
#>         change
#> 1 -0.007963838
#> 2  0.114074796
plot(tr)
#> `geom_smooth()` using formula = 'y ~ x'
